title: IsDComplete Definition
content: **IsDComplete**: A set A is d-complete if every sufficiently large integer is the sum of distinct elements of A with no element dividing another (a divisibility antichain).
mathContext: The concept of d-completeness was introduced by Erdős in 1992, combining two classical conditions: (1) *completeness* — every large integer is a sum of distinct elements (like binary representation), and (2) *antichain* — no summand divides another in the divisibility partial order. The formalization uses Filter.Eventually atTop to express 'sufficiently large', Finset for the finite subset, IsAntichain (· ∣ ·) for the divisibility antichain condition, and Finset.sum id for the sum. This is strictly stronger than ordinary completeness: {1, 2, 4, 8, ...} is complete (binary) but not d-complete since 1 | 2 | 4 | ⋯.
prerequisites: divisibility and partial orders on ℕ
the notion of a complete sequence

title: Powers23 Set
content: **Powers23**: The set {2^k · 3^l : k, l ≥ 0} = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 16, 18, ...}. These are exactly the 3-smooth numbers (positive integers whose only prime factors are 2 and 3).
mathContext: The 3-smooth numbers (also called regular numbers in Babylonian mathematics) are exactly the set {2^k · 3^l}. They form a multiplicative lattice under divisibility: 2^a·3^b ≤ 2^c·3^d iff a ≤ c and b ≤ d. This 2-dimensional lattice structure is what makes the antichain property tractable — elements form an antichain when their exponent pairs are incomparable in the product order on ℕ². The asymptotic count of 3-smooth numbers up to N is Θ((log N)²), so they become increasingly sparse, making d-completeness non-obvious.

title: Closure Under Doubling
content: **double_mem_Powers23**: If n ∈ Powers23, then 2n ∈ Powers23. This is the key closure property: 2^k·3^l becomes 2^{k+1}·3^l.
mathContext: This closure property is the engine of the even-case induction. Multiplying by 2 shifts the 2-adic exponent k → k+1 while preserving the 3-adic exponent l. The proof is one line: from ⟨k, l, rfl⟩ produce ⟨k+1, l, by ring⟩. Combined with antichain_double, this shows the entire 'doubling transformation' (multiply all summands by 2) maps valid d-complete representations to valid d-complete representations, reducing n to n/2.
prerequisites: closure of a set under an operation

title: Divisibility Characterization
content: **Powers23_dvd_iff**: For 2^k₁·3^l₁ to divide 2^k₂·3^l₂, we need BOTH k₁ ≤ k₂ AND l₁ ≤ l₂. This follows from unique factorization via coprimality of 2 and 3.
mathContext: This theorem characterizes divisibility in the multiplicative monoid generated by {2, 3} as the product partial order on ℕ². The proof uses coprimality: since gcd(2,3) = 1, we have 2^a | (2^b · 3^c) implies 2^a | 2^b (by Nat.Coprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_right). The 2-adic and 3-adic valuations are independent. This is Aristotle-verified code using Nat.pow_dvd_pow_iff_le_right and coprimality lifting. The iff makes antichains easy to detect: exponent pairs (k₁,l₁) and (k₂,l₂) are incomparable iff neither dominates componentwise.

title: Antichain Pairs
content: **Powers23_antichain_pair**: When k₁ < k₂ but l₂ < l₁ (exponents 'cross'), neither element divides the other. This creates antichain pairs.
mathContext: This is the key structural lemma: two elements of Powers23 are incomparable under divisibility iff their exponent pairs are incomparable in the product order on ℕ². The crossing condition (k₁ < k₂, l₂ < l₁) means neither (k₁,l₁) ≤ (k₂,l₂) nor (k₂,l₂) ≤ (k₁,l₁). The proof is a one-line application of Powers23_dvd_iff and omega. This generalizes: for B-smooth numbers {p₁^{a₁}···p_r^{a_r}}, the antichain condition becomes incomparability in the r-dimensional product order on ℕ^r.

title: Largest Power of 3
content: **largestPow3**: Returns 3^(⌊log₃ n⌋), the largest power of 3 not exceeding n. Used in the odd case: subtracting this from an odd n gives an even remainder.
mathContext: The function largestPow3(n) = 3^(Nat.log 3 n) computes the greedy 3-adic approximation. For the odd case of induction, we subtract an odd member of Powers23 to make the remainder even. Pure powers of 3 are the natural choice: they are odd (pow_three_odd), they belong to Powers23, and the greedy choice maximizes progress. The three supporting lemmas verify: largestPow3 ≤ n (by Nat.pow_log_le_self), largestPow3 > 0 (by positivity), and largestPow3 ∈ Powers23 (by pow_three_mem_Powers23).

title: Powers of 3 are Odd
content: **pow_three_odd**: All powers of 3 are odd. Proof by induction: 3^0 = 1 is odd; if 3^n is odd, then 3^{n+1} = 3·3^n is odd·odd = odd.
mathContext: This parity fact bridges the multiplicative and additive aspects of the proof. Since 3 ≡ 1 (mod 2), all powers 3^l ≡ 1 (mod 2) are odd. Subtracting an odd power of 3 from an odd n gives an even remainder. The parity trick is specific to the {2,3} case — for {3,5} or {5,7} all generators are odd, so there is no clean parity separation, which is why the general conjecture is harder.

title: Parity Argument
content: **odd_sub_largest_pow3_even**: For odd n > 1, n - largestPow3(n) is even. Since both n and 3^k are odd, odd - odd = even.
mathContext: The proof uses Nat.even_sub (requiring largestPow3 n ≤ n) and the equivalence: the difference is even iff the parities match. Since both n (given as Odd) and largestPow3 n (by pow_three_odd) are odd, both fail the Even test, so the biconditional holds by tauto. This is the structural core of why coprimality of 2 and 3 enables d-completeness: generator 3 provides odd elements for parity adjustment, while generator 2 provides the doubling operation.

title: Main Representation Axiom
content: **powers23_repr** (axiom): Every n ≥ 1 has a d-complete representation as a sum of distinct antichain elements from Powers23.
mathContext: This is the core inductive argument, axiomatized because the full proof requires delicate bookkeeping of Finset operations through nested transformations. The induction: (1) Base: small cases. (2) Even n = 2m: IH gives m = ∑S with S antichain; then n = ∑(2·S) and 2·S is antichain (antichain_double) in Powers23 (double_mem_Powers23). (3) Odd n: let p = largestPow3(n); remainder r = n-p is even (odd_sub_largest_pow3_even); IH gives r = ∑S' with S' antichain of even elements; then n = p + ∑S' and {p}∪S' is antichain because p is odd and S' elements are even (odd numbers cannot divide even numbers in ℕ). Aristotle flagged this as an unexpected axiom.

title: Main Theorem
content: **powers_2_3_dComplete**: The set {2^k · 3^l} is d-complete. Every positive integer is the sum of distinct elements with no divisibility relations.
mathContext: The theorem unfolds IsDComplete to Filter.eventually_atTop and provides N₀ = 1, using powers23_repr for ALL n ≥ 1. This is stronger than d-completeness (which only requires 'sufficiently large' n). The proof is a one-liner: ⟨1, fun n hn => powers23_repr n hn⟩. First proved by Jansen using even/odd induction. Erdős considered this elegant and asked whether it extends to arbitrary coprime triples — leading to the OPEN general conjecture.

crossReferences.description: Complete sequences from digit-restricted sums — sibling problem studying when multi-base digit sets form complete sequences
Distinct subset sums (Conway-Guy) — studies additive structure of exponentially-growing sets, with powers of 2 as extremal examples

prerequisites: assembling the main theorem in Lean

title: Pairwise Coprime and PowersABC
content: **PairwiseCoprime**: Three integers a, b, c are pairwise coprime if gcd(a,b) = gcd(b,c) = gcd(a,c) = 1. **PowersABC**: The generalized set {a^i · b^j · c^k}.
mathContext: Pairwise coprimality is necessary: if gcd(a,b) = p > 1, then the chain 1 | p | p² | ⋯ embeds in PowersABC, and any representation using multiple powers of p violates the antichain condition. For pairwise coprime {a,b,c}, the set PowersABC forms a 3-dimensional multiplicative lattice, with divisibility equivalent to componentwise ≤ on exponent triples (i₁,j₁,k₁) ≤ (i₂,j₂,k₂).

title: General Conjecture
content: **erdos_123_conjecture** (OPEN): For any pairwise coprime a, b, c > 1, is {a^i · b^j · c^k} d-complete? This remains unsolved despite progress on specific cases.
mathContext: The OPEN conjecture generalizes from {2,3} to arbitrary pairwise coprime triples. The difficulty is that the parity argument relies on 2 being a generator. For triples like {5,7,11} (all odd), there is no clean modular decomposition — subtracting a power of one generator from another doesn't change parity. Erdős-Lewin (1996) proved {3,5,7} using residue analysis mod small numbers, but the method doesn't obviously extend. Erdős called this a 'nice and difficult' problem.

title: Erdős-Lewin Result and Two-Generator Special Case
content: **erdos_lewin_357** (axiom): Erdős-Lewin (1996) proved {3^i · 5^j · 7^k} is d-complete. **powers_2_3_special_case**: PowersABC(2,3,1) = Powers23, connecting the two-generator case to the general framework.
mathContext: The Erdős-Lewin 1996 paper proved d-completeness for {3,5,7} without parity tricks, using residue analysis modulo small numbers. The companion theorem powers_2_3_special_case converts between Powers23 and PowersABC(2,3,1) via ext and set manipulation, showing the two-generator case is a special case of the general framework with c = 1.

title: Scaling Preserves Divisibility
content: **dvd_iff_two_mul_dvd**: Divisibility is preserved by uniform scaling: a | b iff 2a | 2b.
mathContext: The multiplicative cancellation property: since 2 > 0, a | b iff 2a | 2b. Forward direction: Nat.mul_dvd_mul_left 2. Reverse: Nat.mul_dvd_mul_iff_left with 0 < 2. This algebraic fact is the core reason the doubling transformation preserves antichains.
prerequisites: scaling a set by a constant factor

title: Antichain Doubling
content: **antichain_double**: If S is a divisibility antichain, then {2s : s ∈ S} is also an antichain. Combined with double_mem_Powers23, this preserves d-complete structure.
mathContext: The proof uses Finset.image (2 * ·) to form 2S, then extracts original elements a, b, proves a ≠ b (from 2a ≠ 2b by injectivity), and applies the original antichain hypothesis via dvd_iff_two_mul_dvd. This is the structural heart of the even-case induction: given m = ∑S with S antichain, we get 2m = ∑(2S) with 2S antichain. The general principle — uniform scaling preserves antichains — holds for any scaling factor, not just 2.
prerequisites: the image of a set under doubling (Finset.image)
